chunks: What the Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, informed me of, from Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Faḍḍāl, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurārah, who said:

I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام that some people say: the inner part of the two ears is part of the face, and their outer part is part of the head. He said: “There is neither washing nor wiping upon them.”

The Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, said: Washing the face and the forearms in wudu (ablution) is once, up to his statement: and he does not take fresh water anew for the wiping; rather, he uses for it the remaining moisture of the wudu (ablution). We have already clarified what pertains to that. Then he said: Whoever errs in wudu (ablution) and puts the washing of his hands before washing his face must return and wash his face, then repeat washing his hands. Likewise, if he puts washing his left hand before his right hand, it is obligatory for him to return to washing his right hand and then repeat washing his left hand. Likewise, if he puts wiping his feet before wiping his head, he must return and wipe his head, then repeat wiping his feet.

That which indicates this is the verse, which is His saying, Most High: “When you rise for salat (prayer), wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and wipe your heads and your feet up to the ankles.”

A group of grammarians have said that the wāw necessitates sequence; among them are al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām and others. If it necessitates sequence, then it is not permissible to put some limbs before others. The verse also indicates this from another angle, which is that He said: “When you rise for salat (prayer), then wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows,” thus making washing the face obligatory immediately after rising for salat (prayer) by the indication of the fāʾ in His saying: “then wash.” There is no disagreement that the fāʾ indicates immediate succession. Once it is established that beginning wudu (ablution) with the face is obligatory, this is established for the remaining limbs as well; because the Ummah is between two positions: one saying there is no sequence and permitting one to begin with the feet first and conclude with the face, and another saying that beginning wudu (ablution) with the face is obligatory and requiring the same for the rest of the limbs.

If someone were to say, according to this approach, that the fāʾ in the verse in this place is not for immediate succession, but rather for consequence, and that the fāʾ which indicates immediate succession is like the statement of one who says, “Strike Zayd, then ʿAmr,” while the fāʾ in the verse functions in consequence like the statement of one who says, “If Zayd comes, then honor him,” and that the difference between the two fāʾs is that when the fāʾ enters into a consequence clause it is not valid to sever the speech from it, whereas if it is for immediate succession it is valid to sever the speech—do you not see that in your saying, “Strike Zayd, then ʿAmr,” it is valid to restrict yourself to saying, “Strike Zayd,” whereas in your saying, “If Zayd comes, then honor him,” it is not valid to restrict yourself to the condition alone? We say: there is no difference between the two fāʾs in the language; because there is no ambiguity that the fāʾ in the language entails immediate succession, so long as it is not part of the word itself. There is no difference in this entailment, as we have mentioned, between its being in a consequence clause or in coordination; because in the saying of one who says, “If Zayd enters, then give him a dirham,” the fāʾ therein necessitates immediate succession even though it is in a consequence clause, for once the entry has occurred from him, he deserves the giving—just as in the saying of one who says, “Strike Zayd, then ʿAmr,” when striking Zayd occurs, it becomes necessary that he strike ʿAmr. So how can a difference between the two fāʾs be imagined? And the sunnah (prophetic tradition) also indicates the obligation of sequence.

key_terms.التَّرْتِيبِ: the required sequence and ordering of the acts of wudu (ablution)
key_terms.السُّنَّةِ: the sunnah (prophetic tradition) as further evidence for the ruling
key_terms.الْفَاءِ: the Arabic particle understood here as indicating immediate succession
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: the ritual ablution discussed throughout the report
key_terms.غَسْلٌ: washing, as applied to the required washed limbs in wudu (ablution)
key_terms.مَسْحٌ: wiping, as applied to the head and feet in wudu (ablution)
key_terms.نَدَاوَةَ: the remaining moisture from wudu (ablution) used for wiping rather than fresh water

ai.seo_question: Does wudu (ablution) require washing and wiping in a fixed order, and are the ears included in it?
ai.summary: This report states that the ears are neither to be washed nor wiped in wudu (ablution). It also establishes the obligation of sequence in wudu (ablution), arguing from the wording of the Qur'anic verse and from linguistic analysis that the limbs must be performed in order, with any misordered act requiring correction and repetition from the point of error.
